newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Pacific economic miracle to continue - survey.
newsitem.headline: Asia Pacific economic miracle to continue - survey.

text.p: Asia Pacific countries are poised to repeat their phenomenal growth of the past decade well into the 21st century, a United Nations body said on Wednesday.

The 1997 survey by the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) said strong world and regional trade and an influx of foreign capital would ensure the region's gross domestic product (GDP) growth stayed between 5.1 and 6.7 percent for the next 20 years.

World GDP growth over the period was projected at between 2.5 and 2.7 percent. Growth for the European Union was seen at 1.5 to 1.6 percent and growth for the United States at 2.1 to 2.4 percent, it said.
"Developing countries in the ESCAP region have increased their share of world trade, private financial flows and foreign direct investment," ESCAP, which is U.N.-affiliated, said.
Their value of trade in goods and services rose to 27 percent of world GDP in 1993 compared to 11 percent in 1971.

But the survey warned that a closer relationship with the global trading community brought with it some problems, such as linking of trade with other issues such as labour welfare, environment and human rights.
"It is important to ensure that such issues are not misused as non-tariff barriers against developing countries," it said.

ESCAP also said that several Asian countries such as China, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, South Korea and Thailand had been targetted for anti-dumping actions by developed countries at one time or another.

"The use of anti-dumping measures as a protective device should be strongly discouraged, particularly because many developing countries may find it difficult to seek relief through costly dispute settlement procedures," ESCAP said.
The commission said developed countries should also avoid the use of national laws to manage trade in order to secure a bilateral trade balance.
ESCAP said intra-regional trade had also grown substantially in recent years.
Exports of merchandise among developing countries in the region grew to 40 percent of their total exports in 1995 from 25 percent in 1980.
But it said regional cooperation agreements, other than the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), had not made much progress with trade liberalisation.
"The efforts in this direction need to be further intensified," ESCAP said. "Initiatives should strive towards a reasonable degree of equity in the distribution of gains."
ESCAP noted that portfolio flow of equity investment from international investors into emerging markets rose to $39 billion in 1995 from a mere $100 million in 1985.
Turning to foreign direct investment (FDI), ESCAP said funds from private sources to developing countries increased to $167 billion in 1995 from $25 billion in 1987.
ESCAP said projected moderate international interest rates would favour member countries as investors diversified their portfolios in order to benefit from the region's high growth.

To keep up the growth, ESCAP said other measures were needed, including greater development of human resources and an improvement in health and educational services along with a more efficient and transparent administration.
